paras.text: Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes due the presence of pi (π) bond in the alkene molecules. Such reactions in which unsaturated compounds are converted into saturated compounds, are called addition reactions. When addition reaction of alkenes is initiated by electrophile, this addition is specifically called electrophilic addition.

16.5.6 Reactivity of Alkenes

Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes due the presence of pi (π) bond in the alkene molecules. The overlap of atomic orbitals forming the pi bond is not as effective as that in sigma (δ) bonds. Thus, pi bond is weaker than a sigma bond and more easily broken. The electron density of pi bond lies above and below the bond axis. It is therefore, more exposed and easily accessible to an external electrophilic (electron seeking) reagent, commonly known as electrophile. It is, therefore, favorable for alkenes to add an electrophile across the double bond by breaking the weak pi bond to form strong sigma bonds and to produce a saturated compound. Such reactions in which unsaturated compounds are converted into saturated compounds, are called addition reactions. When addition reaction of alkenes is initiated by electrophile, this addition is specifically called electrophilic addition.

16.5.7 Reactions of Alkenes

16.5.7.1 Hydrogenation (Addition of Hydrogen)

Alkenes readily add hydrogen to form alkanes in the presence of finely divided catalyst such as nickel, platinum or palladium at a temperature of 200–250°C and under moderate pressure (1–5 atm). This is called catalytic hydrogenation and reaction occurs on the surface of catalyst. The reaction is exothermic and the heat released during hydrogenation of an alkene is called heat of hydrogenation.

Preparation of vegetable ghee from vegetable oil is an example of catalytic hydrogenation at industrial scale. The catalyst used in this process is Raney Nickel after the name of M. Raney, who developed this catalyst.

16.5.7.2 Hydrohalogenation

Alkenes react with hydrogen halide (halogen acids: HCl, HBr or HI) to form an addition product, the alkyl halides (or haloalkanes). The order of reactivity of halogen acids increases down the group.

When the alkene is symmetric (as in the case of ethene), only single product is formed. However if the alkene is asymmetric, two different isomeric products are possible. For example, propene can react with HBr in the following two ways.

However, experimentally it has been found that 2–bromopropane is the major product. In fact this is in accordance with the Markovnikov’s rule, which states that; when an asymmetric reagent is added to an asymmetric alkene, the positive part of the molecule attaches itself to that carbon atom involved in the double bond, holding greater number of hydrogen atoms.

16.5.7.3 Hydration

Alkenes can add a molecule of water across the double bond to form alcohol. This process is known as hydration. Direct hydration of alkene can be accomplished by acid-catalyzed addition of water at 100°C. The most commonly used acids to catalyze this reaction are sulfuric acid and phosphoric acid.

16.5.5.2 Dehydrohalogenation of Alkyl Halides

When an alkyl halide is heated with alcoholic solution of KOH or NaOH, hydrogen and halogen are eliminated which results in the formation of an alkene.

16.5.6 Reactivity of Alkenes

Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes due the presence of pi (π) bond in the alkene molecules. The overlap of atomic orbitals forming the pi bond is not as effective as that in sigma (δ) bonds. Thus, pi bond is weaker than a sigma bond and more easily broken. The electron density of pi bond lies above and below the bond axis. It is therefore, more exposed and easily accessible to an external electrophilic (electron seeking) reagent, commonly known as electrophile. It is, therefore, favorable for alkenes to add an electrophile across the double bond by breaking the weak pi bond to form strong sigma bonds and to produce a saturated compound. Such reactions in which unsaturated compounds are converted into saturated compounds, are called addition reactions. When addition reaction of alkenes is initiated by electrophile, this addition is specifically called electrophilic addition.

16.5.7 Reactions of Alkenes

16.5.7.1 Hydrogenation (Addition of Hydrogen)

Alkenes readily add hydrogen to form alkanes in the presence of finely divided catalyst such as nickel, platinum or palladium at a temperature of 200–250°C and under moderate pressure (1–5 atm). This is called catalytic hydrogenation and reaction occurs on the surface of catalyst. The reaction is exothermic and the heat released during hydrogenation of an alkene is called heat of hydrogenation.

Preparation of vegetable ghee from vegetable oil is an example of catalytic hydrogenation at industrial scale. The catalyst used in this process is Raney Nickel after the name of M. Raney, who developed this catalyst.

16.5.7.2 Hydrohalogenation

Alkenes react with hydrogen halide (halogen acids: HCl, HBr or HI) to form an addition product, the alkyl halides (or haloalkanes). The order of reactivity of halogen acids increases down the group.

When the alkene is symmetric (as in the case of ethene), only single product is formed. However if the alkene is asymmetric, two different isomeric products are possible. For example, propene can react with HBr in the following two ways.

However, experimentally it has been found that 2–bromopropane is the major product. In fact this is in accordance with the Markovnikov’s rule, which states that; when an asymmetric reagent is added to an asymmetric alkene, the positive part of the molecule attaches itself to that carbon atom involved in the double bond, holding greater number of hydrogen atoms.

16.5.7.3 Hydration

Alkenes can add a molecule of water across the double bond to form alcohol. This process is known as hydration. Direct hydration of alkene can be accomplished by acid-catalyzed addition of water at 100°C. The most commonly used acids to catalyze this reaction are sulfuric acid and phosphoric acid.
